Common stock order types investors use: market order (buy/sell at current price), limit order (specific price or better), stop order (trigger price to limit losses), stop-limit order (stop trigger plus price limit), trailing stop order, and after-hours trading order. #stock-orders #investing

A trailing stop order sets a stop price a fixed percent or dollar amount below the stock's high, and the stop price rises as the stock rises but never moves down. Example: 10% trailing stop on a stock bought at $50; at $55 the stop is $49.50, at $60 it is $54. #trailing-stop #stock-orders #investing

Limits of trailing stops: they do not guarantee profits, and in fast or volatile markets a stock can gap down below the stop price with too few buyers, so the order may fill well below the intended stop. They can also trigger too early on high-volatility or low-volume stocks. #trailing-stop #investing #risks

Reasons to place an after-hours trading order: reacting to news/earnings or merger announcements outside market hours, positioning for economic or political data releases, and trading when regular hours (9:30 AM-4:00 PM EST) are inconvenient due to commitments or time zones. #after-hours-trading #stock-orders #investing

After-hours trading risks vs regular hours: higher volatility and wider bid-ask spreads from thin liquidity, limited information, gap risk at the next open, possible order execution delays or unfilled orders, and higher broker fees. #after-hours-trading #investing #risks

Factors for choosing a broker for after-hours trading: whether after-hours access is offered for the desired securities, trading fees and minimum balance requirements, platform/user experience and research tools, and quality of customer support. #broker-selection #after-hours-trading #investing

Paper "Network Hygiene, Incentives, and Regulation: Deployment of Source Address Validation in the Internet" analyzes Spoofer Project crowd-sourced data on SAV (source address validation) deployment. #SAV #Spoofer #paper
For the year ending 1 Aug 2019, 25.2% of tested IPv4 ASes and 32.1% of tested IPv6 ASes had at least one prefix with no outbound SAV filtering of spoofed packets. #SAV #Spoofer #statistics

Spoofer prefix-level SAV stats (year ending Aug 2019): 14.9% of IPv4/24 prefixes with no NAT had no filtering; 12.3% of tested IPv6/40 prefixes did not filter; 6.4% of IPv4 /24 prefixes tested from behind a NAT did not filter. #SAV #Spoofer #statistics

Inbound SAV filtering (spoofed packets claiming a source inside the client's own subnet) is less deployed than outbound: 67.0% of IPv4 ASes and 74.2% of IPv6 ASes had at least one prefix not filtering inbound packets. Tests toggle the 31st bit for IPv4 and the 120th bit for IPv6. #SAV #Spoofer #inbound

Historical comparison: first week of May 2006 saw 18.3% of IPv4/24 prefixes and 20.4% of ASes tested not blocking spoofed-source packets; the year ending Aug 2019 showed 14.9% of IPv4/24 prefixes and 30.5% of ASes — implying SAV deployment has not generally improved. #SAV #Spoofer #trend

Figure 5 finding: no meaningful correlation (Pearson) between IPv4 prefix age (time since first appearance in global BGP table, from Routeviews/RIPE RIS snapshots 2000-2019) and probability of SAV deployment. #SAV #Spoofer #prefix-age

Daemonized Spoofer client sampling is longitudinally sparse: 44% of IPv4 /24 prefixes and 32% of ASes reported measurements in only one week (May 2016–Aug 2019); only 8% of /24 prefixes and 23% of ASes reported in 20+ weeks. Large ISPs (AT&T, Comcast, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom, Charter, Cox) had tests nearly every week. #SAV #Spoofer #sampling

Spoofer per-prefix radix-trie spoofability model (trained chronologically) achieved >90% accuracy; recall rose from ~20% in May 2016 to >80% for IPv6 by Aug 2019 but only 50-70% for IPv4; 76% (IPv4) and 87% (IPv6) of predictions came from the radix trie rather than the global prior. #SAV #Spoofer #modeling

NATs are not a substitute for SAV: in the year ending Aug 2019, 2,783 IPv4 ASes reported tests, 2,418 (86.8%) involving a NAT. Two NAT failure modes: NAT forwards the spoofed source address intact, or rewrites it to the NAT's public address. #SAV #Spoofer #NAT

On 2023/05/21 the user and I had a lengthy conversation about marine wildlife and ecosystem conservation, covering initiatives, enforcement, effectiveness, individual actions, and success stories. #marine-conservation #conversation-log

As of 2021 about 7.5% of the world's oceans were Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), far short of the UN target of 30% by 2030. In 2021 the UK announced plans for a massive MPA around the South Sandwich Islands. #marine-conservation #MPA

The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certifies sustainable fisheries; the Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) does the same for farmed seafood. Enforcement relies on catch limits, gear/size rules, reporting, and international agreements like UNCLOS, with penalties such as fines, license revocation, and market bans (e.g., EU bans imports from countries with poor fisheries management). #marine-conservation #sustainable-fishing

Success stories discussed: humpback whales recovered from ~5,000 in the 1960s to over 80,000 today after the commercial whaling ban; gray whales now ~27,000; North Sea cod up over 300% since 2006 due to sustainable fishing; an Indonesia coral restoration project transplanted 100,000+ corals. #marine-conservation #success-stories

Plastic-reduction examples cited: India's Surat cut plastic waste ~80% in 2020 via a single-use plastics ban; the UK's 5-pence plastic bag charge led to ~80% reduction in bag use. #marine-conservation #plastic-pollution

Individual actions I recommended to the user for helping marine ecosystems: reduce single-use plastic, choose MSC/ASC-certified seafood, lower carbon footprint, join beach cleanups, and support conservation organizations. #marine-conservation #individual-actions

On 2023/06/08 the user asked whether an SEC determination that crypto is a security would force the FDIC to insure it. I answered no: FDIC insurance covers bank deposit accounts (checking, savings, money market deposits, CDs) up to a limit, not digital assets or wallets. #crypto #sec #fdic #investing
Insuring crypto would require an entirely different legal and infrastructural framework from FDIC deposit insurance, since crypto held in digital wallets is not a bank deposit. #crypto #fdic

The SEC decides whether an asset is a security using the Howey Test, from SEC v. W.J. Howey Co. (1946): investment of money, common enterprise, and expectation of profits from the efforts of others. Not all crypto is automatically a security. #sec #crypto

If a crypto asset is a security: the SEC oversees issuance and trading, issuers must register or qualify for an exemption, and detailed business/financial/risk disclosures are required — raising transparency and reducing fraud. #crypto #sec

Crypto treated as a security brings standard investor protections (anti-fraud, anti-manipulation rules) and requires exchanges/trading platforms to register with the SEC as national securities exchanges, ATSs, or broker-dealers. #crypto #sec

Security classification of a crypto asset can affect tax treatment (capital gains, income tax), restrict retail investor access, and raise compliance costs and scrutiny for ICO/token fundraising. #crypto #sec #investing
